summary: Discovery focused on unit economics for Stratos Metrics' planned LLM features. Discussed per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, expected request shapes, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, discounting for reserved capacity, and next steps for benchmarking and pricing follow-up.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Alex from Redwood here with Priya, our solutions engineer. hows everyone today?
[00:06] Maya Patel (Head of ML): Hey Alex, good thanks. we have a tight agenda, mostly cost per token and how batching/caching could help.
[00:12] Diego Alvarez (CTO): yea, we want to understand economics before we pick hosted vs dedicated.
[00:17] Alex Chen: totally. can you walk us through what you plan to build and the request shape? avg tokens in/out, concurrent users, that sort of thing.
[00:27] Maya Patel: sure. our primary feature is semantic search + generate a short insight paragraph. typical user query -> 50 token prompt, 200 token generation. but we have longer workflows too, sometimes 1k tokens. expected p50 around 250 tokens per request.
[00:40] Noah Rivers (Finance): from finance perspective we have a hard monthly budget of $18k for inference to start, could increase with traction but need predictability.
[00:50] Lena Cho (Infra): peak concurrency estimate is 120 qps during trading hours, baseline 15 qps otherwise. stateful caching might reduce that but seems high.
[01:00] Priya Rao (SE): ok good detail. couple of levers here: batching at the runtime layer, prefix/KV caching for repeated documents or context, and model quantization / model choice. these change unit cost and latency tradeoffs.
[01:12] Diego Alvarez: can you quantify? like per-token cost hosted vs dedicated?
[01:16] Alex Chen: high-level: our hosted API pricing list is per 1k tokens, and then Reserved/Dedicated comes with committed throughput discounts. rough ballpark, for the families you're looking at, hosted list might be $0.6 to $1.0 per 1k input+output tokens depending on model tier. Dedicated with reserved capacity often drops effective unit to 40-60% of hosted list if you commit to monthly capacity. I'll send exact tiers.
[01:36] Maya Patel: that's a big range. explain the batching impact — e.g., if we group requests, how much do we save?
[01:42] Priya Rao: batching reduces per-request overhead. if your average request is short, batching many into a single attention pass amortizes the kernel cost. practical savings vary: for small short responses we often see 30-70% token cost reduction with aggressive batching, but latency increases depending on queue depth. for low-latency use cases you tune batch size and max wait.
[02:05] Alex Chen: important note — our smart routing will respect latency SLOs; we won't batch beyond configured max latency. you can set e.g., 10 ms, 50 ms, 200 ms caps.
[02:14] Lena Cho: you mentioned KV cache / prefix cache, how does that work for us? we have many repeated context blocks per client.
[02:20] Priya Rao: KV cache is for autoregressive decoding — if you're reusing the same context across requests (like same document embeddings or prior chat history), prefix caching avoids recomputing earlier layers. for your search+summary flow, if you attach a cached passage or static system prompt, that can cut generation compute 20-60% depending on reuse rate.
[02:39] Diego Alvarez: ok so rough math: 250 tokens per call, 120 qps peak -> that is huge. what's the hourly cost ballpark?
[02:47] Alex Chen: let's do a quick back of the napkin: 250 tokens * 120 qps = 30k tokens/sec = 108M tokens/hour. at $0.8 per 1k tokens hosted = $86.4k/hour, obviously not feasible. but that's raw worst-case without batching/caching and assuming all real-time. you probably will shard traffic, do caching, and burst capacity.
[03:12] Maya Patel: wow that highlights we need to narrow peak assumptions. the 120 qps is theoretical; real sustained is likely 20-25 qps. Peak short spikes maybe 90-120 for a few minutes.
[03:22] Noah Rivers: that math is scary. that's why we want to model both hosted and dedicated reserve scenarios.
[03:27] Priya Rao: for Dedicated: you reserve a GPU pool and get predictable throughput & unit discounts. Because the hardware is dedicated, your amortized token cost can drop significantly, but you need committed spend (monthly/annual). We can model a 3-6 month ramp and show break-even vs hosted.
[03:43] Diego Alvarez: what's the typical break-even horizon?
[03:45] Alex Chen: depends on utilization. at high utilization (70%+), Dedicated often wins in 4-8 weeks vs hosted list pricing. at low utilization (<40%) the flexibility of hosted is cheaper. We'll run modeled scenarios once we have accurate QPS and token distribution.
[03:58] Lena Cho: curious about tooling — can we simulate workload to estimate effective token/unit cost after batching and cache hits?
[04:04] Priya Rao: yes, Priya here — we can run a lightweight benchmark using your sample prompts. we'll vary concurrency, batch size, and cache hit rates. output will include effective tokens per second, latency percentiles, and cost per 1k effective tokens.
[04:18] Diego Alvarez: what about model variants — do you support smaller models for cheaper routes?
[04:21] Alex Chen: yes, we have model catalog and can route to smaller quantized variants for lower-cost use cases. also automatic fallback is possible: if dedicated pool is saturated we can route to hosted burst or a lower-cost model variant.
[04:33] Maya Patel: security question — if we go Dedicated or Private, how do you handle keys and logs? KMS? audit logs?
[04:40] Alex Chen: for Dedicated/Private we support customer-managed KMS and dedicated audit logging. we also have SOC2 report and can provide SAML SSO for team access. I'll attach security docs in the follow-up.
[04:52] Noah Rivers: for pricing, also include cost variance scenarios: optimistic (high cache hits, batching), baseline, pessimistic (low cache, high concurrency).
[04:58] Priya Rao: noted. we'll include sensitivity analysis and show per-token effective cost ranges.
[05:03] Lena Cho: ops question — any multi-region options for latency? we are in NA with EU users.
[05:07] Alex Chen: yes, hosted is multi-region; Dedicated can be provisioned in region(s) you choose. routing policies can send EU traffic to EU pool to meet data residency/latency.
[05:15] Maya Patel: can you give a concrete example of how batching changes cost? like 50 token prompt -> 200 token response, 1000 RPS but batched to average batch size 8.
[05:23] Priya Rao: rough example: unbatched cost = kernel overhead per request + token decode. when batched at size 8, overhead amortized so compute per-token might drop 40-60%. so your effective tokens paid might be the same but the GPU cycles per token drop. I'll put numbers in the sheet.
[05:39] Diego Alvarez: about QoS, if we reserve capacity and need burst beyond it, how does pricing work for bursts?
[05:45] Alex Chen: bursts can go to hosted at pay-as-you-go pricing, or to a lower-cost standby pool. we also support burst credits on some contracts; details in the pricing sheet.
[05:55] Maya Patel: for the bench we will provide representative prompt set, including long-form 1k token cases.
[05:59] Priya Rao: great — please include distribution: percent short vs long, and expected cache hit rate.
[06:05] Noah Rivers: timeline — finance wants a recommendation by end of month.
[06:08] Alex Chen: ok we'll prioritize the cost model. next steps recap: I'll send pricing and security docs; Priya will run hosted benchmark and share results; schedule POC scoping if numbers look good.
[06:18] Maya Patel: sounds good. one more quick Q — do you support model quantization levels we can test? like 4-bit vs 8-bit?
[06:24] Priya Rao: yes we support multiple quantization profiles; results vary per model. we'll include expected quality-impact notes in the benchmarking report.
[06:33] Diego Alvarez: perfect. thanks everyone.
[06:35] Alex Chen: thanks all. we'll follow up with action items.
[06:37] (call ends)
notes: Meeting had some minor transcription errors (names/misheard acronyms). Emphasis on establishing realistic peak assumptions and running a short benchmark. Customer budget constraint ($18k/month) drove much of the discussion. Redwood to provide pricing tiers and benchmark results.
